newsitem.title: USA: US stocks seen listless in shortened holiday trade.
newsitem.headline: US stocks seen listless in shortened holiday trade.

text.p: U.S. stocks should open lightly mixed Tuesday, with very light turnover and no major market moves expected in an abbreviated session before the Christmas holiday tomorrow.
The Dow Industrials rose five points to about 6489 on Monday in very thin trading, with many Wall Street players already away on vacation.
"We'll probably just be drifting up or down a little bit in very low volume. I expect more of yesterday," said Hildegard Zagorski, Prudential Securities market analyst.
The March contract of futures of the Standard & Poor's 500 Index was flat at 754.10 ahead of the opening. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was off 1/32 to yield 6.59 percent.
The New York Stock Exchange, Nasdaq and the American Stock Exchange all will close early today at 1300 EST/1800 GMT and will remain closed tomorrow, December 25.

Peter Cardillo, director of research for Westfalia Investments, said, "We'll probably be in much of a state of limbo today ... We should have a mixed opening but I expect a higher close in a small Santa Claus rally."
He added, "Banking stocks have been in the spotlight and that could continue since interest rates seem to have settled down."
At 0900 EST/1400 GMT, BTM/Schroders reports store sales for the week ended December 21. Sales rose 0.7 percent in the prior week.

Tokyo stock markets fell sharply on worries about Japan's economic prospects, with the key Nikkei average of 225 stocks sliding more than 2.0 percent in late trading to close down 528.75 to 19.161.71, its lowest level since December 19, 1995.
London stocks ended a mostly featureless session on a higher note, with the FTSE 100 index scoring its third consecutive advance. The index rose 5.2 to 4,092.4.
U.S. stocks in London were very little changed, with many market players absent for the holidays.
The dollar was steady in tiny ranges ahead of the opening of trading. Most experts expect very thin trading because of the holidays.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said James Robinson, who resigned as chairman of the American Express financial services empire three years ago, is tapping old associates to possibly set up a private equity fund of perhaps $200 million.
